description: We are a team of three pre-final-year Computer Science and Engineering students from Amal Jyothi College of Engineering, Kerala, India. Driven by curiosity, innovation, and a shared passion for space technology, we aim to combine our technical skills and creativity to explore meaningful solutions to real-world challenges. Through NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are excited to contribute to the future of lunar exploration with LUNA NAV.
summary:
LUNA NAV (Lunar Navigation, Illumination & Communication Analysis) helps people explore potential landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. Choose a site, date, and observation window to view the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon. Live mode retrieves celestial positions from NASA/JPL Horizons; sample mode provides clearly labelled illustrative data.

The dashboard displays sky directions, elevation timelines, estimated sunlight and Earth line-of-sight periods, and side-by-side comparisons of up to three site-date plans. A schematic lunar explorer and plain-language user guide make the results easier to understand.

LUNA NAV is a screening and educational tool. It does not calculate terrain obstruction, surface power generation, landing safety, or a verified communications link budget.
details:
LUNA NAV — Lunar Navigation, Illumination & Communication Analysis

LUNA NAV is a web application for exploring potential landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. It helps users compare how the Sun and Earth appear from different places and at different times.

Choose a reference location or enter coordinates, set a local date and time, and select an evaluation window. In live mode, a Next.js API route requests Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons using the selected lunar location as the observer. The app displays the results in a sky view and elevation timeline, and lets users compare up to three site-date plans. A clearly labelled sample mode is available to demonstrate the interface when live data is unavailable.

The project is intended to make lunar illumination and Earth line of sight easier to explore for mission planners, students, educators, and the public. Side-by-side comparisons help users see trade-offs between scenarios without hiding the measurements behind a single ranking.

We used Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, SVG, and Three.js. Site information is stored in JSON, and the app uses Next.js API routes for server-side data requests. We did not use a database or specialized hardware.

Our approach combines a 2D sky view, timelines, a 3D lunar explorer, and scenario comparison in one tool. We considered clarity for non-specialists, local-time and UTC handling, transparent separation of live and illustrative data, and the limits of the available science. The current app does not calculate LOLA terrain obstruction, power generation, landing safety, or a verified communications link budget; its visibility results are geometric estimates.

GitHub repository link: https://github.com/albert-8421/LunaNav.git
